card.name: Pandanggo sa Ilaw
card.tagline: The Filipino candle dance — three oil lamps balanced on head and hands, the dancer never spills a drop.
card.profile: Pandanggo sa Ilaw — the dance of light — is the most iconic of the Philippines' Spanish colonial-era folk dances, originating in Mindoro province. The dancer balances three lit tinghoy (oil lamps in coconut shells) — one on the head and one in each hand — and dances in 3/4 time, moving with such control that the flames never flicker, the oil never spills. The dance dramatises Philippine fishermen returning home from sea using lamps as signal lights, transforming a maritime practical act into a luminous national symbol.
card.insight: Pandanggo sa Ilaw is named the unofficial national dance of the Philippines by the Cultural Center of the Philippines, and it is taught in every Filipino school as part of the elementary curriculum. The three lit oil lamps — balanced on the head and two extended hands — require years of practice; advanced dancers can perform pandanggo while squatting low, spinning, and even kneeling, with the flames never flickering.

card.profile_long: Pandanggo sa Ilaw is a prominent Philippine folk dance that traces its roots to the Spanish colonial period. It is a specialized form of the Pandanggo, a dance that arrived in the Philippines from Spain and became widely popular across the archipelago. While the term 'Pandanggo' was used in the 18th century to describe any dance that was considered jovial and lively, the specific variant known as Pandanggo sa Ilaw—or 'fandango with lights'—emerged from Lubang Island in the province of Mindoro. The defining feature of this dance is the performer's skill in balancing lit oil lamps, known as tinghoy, on their head and in their hands while executing movements. This requires immense focus and control, as the dance is performed in a manner that keeps the flames steady. The dance is not merely a display of balance but a cultural expression that has integrated into both social and religious life in the Philippines. It is often performed at social gatherings, where the music and the dancers' movements create a lively atmosphere. In these settings, the dance may continue through several repetitions, with musicians increasing the tempo until the dancers are exhausted. Beyond its social role, the Pandanggo has deep connections to religious practice. It is performed during processions and rituals, such as the procession of St. Martha and the Sayaw sa Obando, which is specifically for childless couples. The evolution of the dance from its Spanish origins to its current form reflects the way local communities in the Philippines adapted foreign influences into their own unique traditions. While the Spanish Fandango itself was eventually superseded by Flamenco in Spain, the Philippine Pandanggo has persisted as a living tradition. It serves as a testament to the cultural synthesis that occurred during the Hispanic period, maintaining its popularity through both secular celebrations and sacred observances across various localities in the Philippines.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance evolved from the Spanish Fandango, which was introduced to the Philippines during the Hispanic period. Pandanggo sa Ilaw specifically originated on Lubang Island, Mindoro.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves performers balancing lit oil lamps on their head and in their hands. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by castanets and clapping. Musicians play faster and faster after each repetition until the dancers are exhausted.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed at social gatherings and religious processions. Dancers use oil lamps (tinghoy).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used in social gatherings and religious rituals, including processions for St. Martha and the Sayaw sa Obando for childless couples.
sections.regional_variants: There are many versions of the Pandanggo, with each locality having its own. Oasioas is another popular version.

claims.text: Pandanggo sa Ilaw, which originated in Lubang Island, Mindoro, involves the dancers performing while balancing lights.
The dance evolved from Fandango, a Spanish folk dance, which arrived in the Philippines during the Hispanic period.
Pandanggo is still danced by many people but mostly in religious rituals and processions.
The dance is accompanied by castanets.
Local dancers have many ways of doing the Pandanggo, but there is one thing in common between different versions: they have gay and sprightly figures.
The musicians play faster and faster after each repetition until the dancers are exhausted.
